paras: The lynching of a discharged soldier and a woman near Pickens, Mississippi, was the reported killing of two unnamed Black people on the outskirts of Pickens, Holmes County, on or shortly before May 12, 1919. According to a dispatch from Durant, the lynching followed the man's reported admission that he had hired the woman to write an "improper note" to a young woman at Pickens. The National Association for the Advancement of Colored People later cited the case in a telegram pressing Governor Theodore G. Bilbo over Mississippi's run of lynchings.

The only narrative account, datelined Durant, May 12, said a "race soldier recently discharged from the army and a woman" had been lynched in the outskirts of Pickens, citing reports received that night by Marshal J. S. Konlofer. The dispatch said the lynching "is said to have followed admission by the man" that he had paid the woman to write the note, without naming the young woman or giving her race. It did not name the victims, describe the lynchers, or say how the two were killed.

No report of an inquest, arrests or prosecution appears in the coverage. On May 24 the NAACP, through its secretary John R. Shillady, telegraphed Governor Bilbo that "a Negro soldier and a Negro woman were alleged to have been lynched near Pickens" about five days before the burning of Lloyd Clay at Vicksburg. The telegram said that as far as the association could learn Mississippi authorities had done nothing in any of the five recent cases, and warned that the state's failure to enforce its laws justified Black migration and made federal intervention inevitable.

In New York, Colonel William Hayward told the Republican County Committee that he had been aroused by reading of a colored man lynched in Durant over a letter to a woman. Recalling the sacrifices of Black soldiers in the war, he said that "if that report is true all the Huns are not in Germany by any means."

Coverage found in the Black press began with the Baltimore Afro-American, which on May 16 listed "MAN AND WOMAN LYNCHED IN MISS" among the week's headlines on its editorial page. The next day the Cleveland Advocate printed the Durant dispatch without comment under "TWO LYNCHED IN MISSISSIPPI," set among Buffalo society notes. The New York Age carried the case on its front page only through Hayward's speech, headlined "Hayward Denounces Reign of Mob Law in the South."

In June the NAACP's release ran as "Mississippi Governor Again Asked If Lynchers Are To Be Prosecuted" in the Dayton Forum on June 6 and the Dallas Express on June 7. That release treated the Pickens killings as one of five Mississippi lynchings in less than three months, while describing them, unlike the wire dispatch, as "alleged."

Hayward's speech, as printed, placed the lynching in Durant and mentioned only a man, whereas the Durant dispatch and the NAACP placed it near Pickens and named two victims. The dispatch dated the report May 12, while the NAACP's chronology, counted back from Lloyd Clay's burning, put the killings about May 9.

reader.title: Lynching of a discharged soldier and a woman near Pickens, Mississippi
bases: The Durant dispatch says a discharged soldier and a woman 'were lynched' outside Pickens after an accusation about a note, and the NAACP counted it among Mississippi lynchings (A2, A4).

Both victims were reported lynched without any legal process after the man's reported admission about an 'improper note' (A2), but no report describes the killers or their number, and the NAACP called the killings 'alleged' (A4).

The only narrative is one Durant wire dispatch (A2); the Afro-American headline (A1), the Hayward speech (A3) and the NAACP telegram (A4) add no independent detail and the NAACP itself calls the lynching 'alleged'.

accounts.label: Durant wire dispatch
accounts.gist: A discharged soldier and a woman were lynched on the outskirts of Pickens, reportedly after the man admitted hiring the woman to write an improper note to a young woman there.

accounts.label: NAACP telegram
accounts.gist: A Negro soldier and a Negro woman were 'alleged to have been lynched near Pickens' five days before Lloyd Clay was burned at Vicksburg, which the May 24 telegram put "ten days ago", and Mississippi authorities had done nothing.

accounts.label: Col. Hayward's speech
accounts.gist: Hayward said he had read that a colored man was lynched in Durant over a letter to a woman, and asked whether the United States was safe for democracy.

framing.detail: The Cleveland Advocate printed the Durant dispatch without comment under 'TWO LYNCHED IN MISSISSIPPI' amid Buffalo society notes.
The Baltimore Afro-American listed 'MAN AND WOMAN LYNCHED IN MISS' among the week's headlines atop its editorial page.
The New York Age front-paged Hayward's speech under 'Hayward Denounces Reign of Mob Law in the South', with the Durant report as his occasion.
The NAACP release, run as 'Mississippi Governor Again Asked If Lynchers Are To Be Prosecuted', used the case to press Bilbo on prosecution.
